g(mn)=∑a∣m​∑b∣n​f(ab)=(∑a∣m​f(a))(∑b∣n​f(b))=g(m)g(n).
(1)
The Möbius function is μ(n)=0 if a prime square divides n, and μ(n)=(−1)r if n is a product of r distinct primes. The Euler totient function ϕ(n) counts residues modulo n coprime to n. From the prime factorizations,
nϕ(n)​=∏p∣n​(1−p1​)=∑d∣n​dμ(d)​.
(2)
Both sides of the second identity are multiplicative, and at a prime power pa,
∑d∣pa​ϕ(d)μ(d)2​=1+p−11​=p−1p​=ϕ(pa)pa​.
(3)

ϕ(n)n​=d∣n∑​ϕ(d)μ(d)2​​.

For a q-ary code with codeword lengths l1​,…,lm​, Kraft inequality is
i=1∑m​q−li​≤1​.
(11)
Choose an infinite random q-ary string with independent uniform symbols. The event that it begins with codeword i has probability q−li​. For a prefix-free code, these events are disjoint, so their probabilities sum to at most one. This proves necessity.

Words: 79 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 79
b OurBigBook.com
If one comma codeword were a prefix of another, its terminal comma would occur inside the longer codeword, contrary to the definition. Thus every comma code is prefix-free. Directly, the disjoint cylinder sets of infinite strings beginning with the respective comma-terminated words have measures q−li​, so their total measure gives Kraft's inequality.
Kraft's inequality does not imply unique decipherability. Over the binary alphabet,
C={0,01,10}
(12)
has Kraft sum 1/2+1/4+1/4=1, but
010=0∣10=01∣0.
(13)
Thus it is not uniquely decipherable.

4I (Automata and Formal Languages)

Words: 167 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 167
4I OurBigBook.com
Fix an effective enumeration of register-machine programs. The nth register machine is Pn​, and its domain
Wn​={x:Pn​ halts on input x}
(14)
is the nth recursively enumerable set. A many-one reduction A≤m​B is a total computable function h satisfying x∈A⟺h(x)∈B. Rice theorem says that every nontrivial property depending only on the computed partial function, or equivalently on an r.e. set in its extensional form, has an undecidable index set.
There is no total equality algorithm: it would decide whether Wn​ is empty by comparing it with a fixed index for the empty set, contradicting Rice's theorem.
There is no partial algorithm that halts exactly when Wm​=Wn​ either. Given e, effectively construct an index h(e) whose machine enumerates nothing unless Pe​(e) halts, after which it enumerates 0. Then
Wh(e)​=∅⟺e∈/K.
(15)
A semialgorithm for equality with a fixed empty index would enumerate the complement of the halting problem K. Since K is r.e., both it and its complement would then be r.e., making K recursive, a contradiction.

For Yμ​∼Poisson(μ), the delta method with g(y)=2y​ gives
Var(g(Yμ​))≈g′(μ)2Var(Yμ​)=μ1​μ=1.
(16)
Thus the transformation stabilizes variance at large μ.
A Gaussian linear model for Y​ treats the transformed observations as having additive constant-variance errors and models E(Y​∣X) as linear. A Poisson regression with square-root link retains the Poisson likelihood and models
E(Y∣X)​=Xβ.
(17)
The two procedures therefore have different likelihoods, fitted means, and constraints; transforming the response is not the same as transforming its conditional mean.

7E (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 126
7E OurBigBook.com
Use a keyhole contour about the negative real axis, indented symmetrically around the pole s=t. The jump of sz−1 across the cut is determined by the chosen branch, and the small and large circular contributions vanish for 0<Rez<1. The residue theorem, with the symmetric indentation interpreted as a Cauchy principal value, gives
PV∫−∞∞​s−tsz−1​ds=πitz−1​.
(25)
Splitting the real axis at zero and substituting s↦−s in the negative part gives two linear relations. Solving them yields, for real 0<z<1,
∫0∞​s+tsz−1​ds=πtz−1csc(πz)​,
(26)
PV∫0∞​s−tsz−1​ds=−πtz−1cot(πz)​.
(27)
Both sides are holomorphic functions of z throughout the vertical strip 0<Rez<1: convergence is locally uniform there, and the trigonometric expressions are holomorphic away from integer poles. The identity theorem therefore extends the identities from real z to the whole strip.

Words: 73 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 73
9A OurBigBook.com
Chemical equilibrium for p+e↔H gives
μH​=μp​+μe​,
(35)
and charge neutrality gives np​=ne​. Insert the nonrelativistic Maxwell-Boltzmann number densities, use mH​c2=mp​c2+me​c2−Ebind​, and neglect the proton correction in the reduced mass. The spin degeneracies cancel in the ground-state approximation. One obtains Saha equation
ne2​nH​​=(me​kB​T2πℏ2​)3/2exp(kB​TEbind​​)​.
(36)
Equivalently, its reciprocal is the ionization ratio. The exponential favors neutral hydrogen as the temperature falls, while the translational phase-space factor favors ionization at high temperature.

a OurBigBook.com
The no-signalling theorem states that any trace-preserving quantum operation performed locally by Bob leaves Alice's reduced density matrix unchanged when Bob's outcome is not communicated:
TrB​[(I⊗EB​)(ρAB​)]=TrB​ρAB​.
(37)
Thus Bob's choice cannot change the statistics of any measurement made by Alice.

Words: 80 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 80
b OurBigBook.com
A unitary cloner with blank state ∣0⟩ would satisfy
U(∣ψ⟩∣0⟩)=∣ψ⟩∣ψ⟩
(38)
for every ∣ψ⟩∈S. For ∣ψ⟩,∣ϕ⟩∈S, preservation of inner products gives
⟨ψ∣ϕ⟩=⟨ψ∣ϕ⟩2.
(39)
Hence every pair is either orthogonal or represents the same state. Conversely, an orthonormal set can be cloned by defining the map on its basis states and extending it to a unitary. Therefore the no-cloning theorem says that a set of pure states is unitarily clonable exactly when its distinct members are mutually orthogonal.

c

Words: 98 Articles: 1
10D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 98
c OurBigBook.com
Let Alice and Bob share the Bell state
∣Φ+⟩=2​∣00⟩+∣11⟩​=2​∣++⟩+∣−−⟩​.
(40)
Alice may measure in the computational basis, remotely preparing Bob's ensemble {∣0⟩,∣1⟩}, or in the Hadamard basis, preparing {∣+⟩,∣−⟩}. Without her outcome, both ensembles have density matrix I/2, as no-signalling requires.
If Bob could clone all four states, the resulting two-qubit ensembles would be
21​(∣00⟩⟨00∣+∣11⟩⟨11∣)
(41)
and
21​(∣++⟩⟨++∣+∣−−⟩⟨−−∣).
(42)
They are distinguishable: a Z⊗Z measurement is perfectly correlated for the first and only equally likely correlated or anticorrelated for the second. Bob could infer Alice's basis choice instantaneously, violating no-signalling. Thus no-signalling implies no-cloning for this set.

A binary cyclic code of odd length n is an ideal of F2​[X]/(Xn−1). For a primitive nth root α, its defining set is the set of powers αi at which every code polynomial vanishes. A BCH code of design distance δ has δ−1 consecutive powers
αb,αb+1,…,αb+δ−2
(43)
in its defining set.
If a nonzero codeword had weight w<δ, write it as c(X)=∑j=1w​cj​Xij​. Evaluation at w consecutive defining roots gives a homogeneous Vandermonde system in the nonzero values cj​αbij​. Its determinant is nonzero because the support elements αij​ are distinct. Thus every cj​ would vanish, a contradiction. This proves the BCH bound
dmin​≥δ​.
(44)

σ(Z)=h=1∏ν​(1−αih​Z)​.

The primitive recursive functions are the smallest class containing zero, successor, and projections and closed under composition and primitive recursion. Addition is defined by
P(m,0)=m,P(m,n+1)=S(P(m,n)),
(52)
and multiplication by
T(m,0)=0,T(m,n+1)=P(T(m,n),m).
(53)
Thus both are primitive recursive directly from the definition. Inductively,
Tk+1​(n1​,…,nk+1​)=T(Tk​(n1​,…,nk​),nk+1​)
(54)
is primitive recursive. For fixed a,
Ea​(0)=1,Ea​(n+1)=T(a,Ea​(n)),
(55)
so Ea​(n)=an is primitive recursive.
Encode (x0​,…,xk−1​) by 2x0​3x1​⋯pkxk−1​​. The exponent functions Mpi​​ decode the coordinates. Therefore
F(N)=∏i=0k−1​pi+1fi​(M2​(N),M3​(N),…,Mpk​​(N))​
(56)
is a primitive recursive one-number encoding of F; the finite product is built from the primitive recursive multiplication and exponentiation just established.
The Fibonacci function is primitive recursive. Encode the pair (B(n),B(n+1)) by
C(n)=2B(n)3B(n+1).
(57)
Starting with C(0)=3, primitive recursion using
C(n+1)=2M3​(C(n))3M2​(C(n))+M3​(C(n))
(58)
constructs C, and B(n)=M2​(C(n)).
There is no universal exponential bound of the stated form. The primitive recursive function
f(n)=2n2
(59)
exceeds Rn for every fixed R>0 once n is sufficiently large.

b OurBigBook.com
The code fits a Bernoulli logistic-regression model. Conditionally on the covariates, the responses are independent with
Yi​∼Bernoulli(pi​),log1−pi​pi​​=xiT​β,
(60)
where the design includes the displayed numerical predictors and indicator columns for factor levels. It maximizes
L(β)=∏i=1889​piYi​​(1−pi​)1−Yi​.
(61)
Akaike information criterion is
AIC=2k−2ℓ(β​),
(62)
where k is the number of fitted parameters. Backward stepwise selection starts from the full model, tentatively removes each eligible term, chooses the removal producing the lowest AIC, and repeats while AIC decreases. It balances fit against model size rather than testing every coefficient at a fixed significance threshold.

The Knaster-Tarski theorem says that the fixed points of a monotone self-map of a complete lattice form a complete lattice. In particular,
lfp(f)=⋀{x:f(x)≤x},gfp(f)=⋁{x:x≤f(x)}.
(81)
For the first formula, let a be the displayed meet. Monotonicity gives f(a)≤f(x)≤x for every prefixed point x, hence f(a)≤a. Then f(f(a))≤f(a), so f(a) is itself prefixed; minimality of a gives a≤f(a). Thus f(a)=a. The dual argument gives the greatest fixed point. Applying the same construction above the join of any family of fixed points, and dually below its meet, supplies joins and meets within the fixed-point set.
A down-set contains every element below any of its members. Arbitrary unions and intersections of down-sets are down-sets. Thus the down-sets of X, ordered by inclusion, have joins given by unions and meets by intersections, so they form a complete lattice.
For the requested counterexample, take
X=[0,1),Y=[0,1]
(82)
with their usual orders. The set X is a down-set in Y, while Y is order-isomorphic to the down-set [0,1/2] of X. They are not isomorphic because Y has a greatest element and X does not.

A proper k-coloring assigns one of k colors to each vertex so adjacent vertices receive different colors. The chromatic number χ(G) is the least such k. Order the vertices arbitrarily and color greedily. At most Δ(G) colors are forbidden by previously colored neighbors, so
χ(G)≤Δ(G)+1​.
(86)
Equality occurs for every possible maximum degree: use K1​ for Δ=0, K2​ for Δ=1, an odd cycle for Δ=2, and KΔ+1​ for every Δ≥3.

A graph is k-connected when it has more than k vertices and remains connected after deletion of fewer than k vertices. In a noncomplete 3-connected graph, choose a vertex v with two nonadjacent neighbors a,b. Since G−{a,b} is connected, take a spanning tree rooted at v and order its vertices so every vertex other than v has a later tree neighbor. Color a and b first with the same color, then greedily color the other vertices in reverse tree order, leaving v last. Every nonfinal vertex has one uncolored neighbor and therefore sees at most Δ−1 colors. At v, the two neighbors a,b share a color, so again at most Δ−1 colors occur. Hence
χ(G)≤Δ(G)​.
(87)
This is the relevant 3-connected case of Brooks' theorem.

χ′(G)=4​.

a OurBigBook.com
The uniformization theorem says that every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally equivalent to exactly one of the Riemann sphere, the complex plane, and the unit disc. A proper simply connected plane domain is noncompact, so it is not the sphere. It cannot be uniformized by the plane: after choosing a point outside the domain, a branch of a square root and then a Möbius transformation would produce a nonconstant bounded entire function, contradicting the Liouville theorem. It is therefore conformally equivalent to the disc, which is the Riemann mapping theorem.

For an irreducible algebraic variety X and p∈X, the local ring OX,p​ consists of germs of rational functions regular on a neighbourhood of p. If X⊆An has ideal I(X), its Zariski tangent space is
Tp​X={v∈kn:dfp​(v)=0 for every f∈I(X)}.

The given variety is the blowup of the affine plane at the origin. On the chart W=0, put W=1; then Y=XZ, so (X,Z) are free affine coordinates. On the chart Z=0, put Z=1; then X=WY, so (W,Y) are free affine coordinates. These two smooth affine-plane charts cover V, hence every point of V is smooth.
If (X,Y)=(0,0), the equation forces
[W:Z]=[X:Y].
(135)
Consequently π restricts to an isomorphism away from the origin, and is therefore birational. Above the origin, however,
π−1(0,0)={(0,0)}×P1,
(136)
so π is not injective and cannot be an isomorphism of algebraic varieties. Birationality gives
k(V)=k(A2)=k(X,Y)​.
(137)
For any morphism φ:V→V′ with V′ affine, its restriction to the exceptional curve E≅P1 is constant: every regular function on a projective line is constant, and the affine coordinate functions of V′ therefore have constant pullbacks. Since E has more than one point, φ is not injective. If V itself were affine, its identity morphism would contradict this conclusion, so V is not affine.
Over C, V is not compact in the Euclidean topology: the sequence (n,0,[1:0]) has no convergent subsequence. Every complex projective variety is Euclidean compact. Since compactness is preserved by homeomorphisms, V cannot be homeomorphic to a projective variety.

Conversely, conformality gives ∣k1​∣=∣k2​∣=0. It permits either k1​=−k2​, which is minimal, or k1​=k2​=0, which is umbilical and nonminimal. On a round sphere, the Gauss map is conformal while both principal curvatures are equal and nonzero. Thus conformality alone does not imply minimality.

No. If the image lies in a great circle, there is a fixed unit vector a with ⟨N,a⟩=0, so a is tangent to S everywhere. The Gauss map is then locally constant, and connectedness makes it constant on all of S, contradicting its image being a great circle.

On a probability space carrying an infinite IID sequence (Xn​) with law m, map ω to (X1​(ω),X2​(ω),…). Its pushforward measure μ satisfies
μ(∏n≥1​An​)=∏n≥1​m(An​)
(141)
for every cylinder set. Cylinder sets form a pi-system generating σ(C), so the sigma-finite uniqueness theorem for measures proves uniqueness. This is the countable product measure m⊗N.
For a cylinder A=A1​×⋯×AN​×R×⋯,
μ(θ−1A)=m(R)m(A1​)⋯m(AN​)=μ(A).

The same generating-class argument extends this equality to every measurable set, so θ is a measure-preserving transformation.
If A=θ−1A, then A=θ−nA for every n, so membership in A is independent of the first n coordinates. Thus A belongs to the tail sigma-algebra. The zero-one law gives μ(A)∈{0,1}, proving that the shift is ergodic.

In the cavity, the rigid condition u(L)=0 gives

−ω2mξ​=p​(0−)−p​(0+),u(0)=iωξ​,

The numerator is the complex conjugate of the denominator, hence ∣R∣=1. No mean acoustic energy can pass through the rigid end, so all incident energy is ultimately reflected.

These are standing-wave resonances of the closed cavity: both the membrane at x=0 and the rigid wall at x=L are velocity nodes, while the pressure field is nontrivial.

away from the resonances sinβ=0. Then R→1, the membrane velocity tends to zero, and the cavity amplitude obtained from the matching equations is O(α−1) relative to the pressure in x<0. The membrane therefore acts as an almost rigid reflecting wall and scarcely excites the cavity.

z(k)=Hkz(0)=VΛkV−1z(0).

If the spectral radius ρ(H)<1, every eigenvalue satisfies ∣λi​∣<1, so Λk→0 and hence z(k)→0 for every initial vector. Conversely, taking z(0) to be an eigenvector of any eigenvalue λ shows that convergence for every initial vector forces λk→0, hence ∣λ∣<1. Therefore
z(k)→0 for all z(0)⟺ρ(H)<1​.
